1.1: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier on 25 February 1304 (Ibn Juzayy's note, vol. I, p. 8) and left on 2 Rajab 725, in June 1325. He was twenty-two in lunar years, twenty-one in ours.
1.2: Ask: where would you most like to travel one day? Why?
1.3: His own words: "I set out alone, having neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer, nor caravan whose party I might join ... My parents being yet in the bonds of life, it weighed sorely upon me to part from them, and both they and I were afflicted with sorrow at this separation" (vol. I, pp. 7-8).
1.4: Pack a real bag together for a pretend journey. What do you really need, and what can stay at home?
1.5: "I braced my resolution to quit all my dear ones, female and male, and forsook my home as birds forsake their nests" (vol. I, p. 8).
1.6: Talk about the Hajj: who in your family has been? What did they see?
2.1: He describes visiting the lighthouse of Alexandria, already partly in ruins (vol. I, p. 18).
2.2: Ask: who is the oldest person you know? What could you learn from them?
2.3: The imam Burhan al-Din the Lame: "You must certainly, if God will, visit my brother Farid al-Din in India, and my brother Rukn al-Din Zakariya in Sind, and my brother Burhan al-Din in China, and when you reach them convey to them a greeting from me" (vol. I, pp. 22-23). The book tells this as a karama, a wonder given to a holy man; the game says only what he said.
2.4: "I was amazed at his prediction, and the idea of going to these countries having been cast into my mind, my wanderings never ceased until I had met these three that he named and conveyed his greeting to them" (vol. I, p. 23).
2.5: Find Morocco, Egypt, India, the Maldives, Indonesia, China and Mali on a map or globe together.
2.6: Ask: have you ever passed on a greeting, 'salam from Grandma'? Why does it make people happy?
3.1: Damascus had endowments (waqf) of many kinds: for freeing prisoners, for travellers (food, clothing and the cost of the journey home), and for paving the streets (vol. I, p. 147).
3.2: In the book the boy is a slave-boy. Slavery was part of every society Ibn Battuta saw, and he owned slaves himself (see the notes in chapters 7 and 11).
3.3: Ask: what do you do when a friend breaks something by accident?
3.4: Is there a 'dish fund' you could make at home: a jar for fixing things or helping someone?
3.6: "This endowment is one of the best of good works, for the boy's master would undoubtedly have beaten him for breaking the dish ... The benefaction is thus indeed a mender of hearts" (vol. I, p. 147).
3.7: Ask your child for one thing they did this week that mended someone's heart.
4.1: Ask: how long do you think the journey took on a camel? (Many weeks.) How long would it take by plane?
4.2: His first Hajj was in 1326; he describes Makkah, the mosque and the Ka'bah at length (vol. I, pp. 188-191 and after). He made the Hajj again on his way home in 1348 (vol. IV, p. 920).
4.3: Read 22:27 together. Ask: why do people come from every land to the same place?
4.4: Talk through the days of Hajj with pictures or a video together.
4.5: Ask: what would you want to see next, after Makkah?
4.6: Ask: why do you think all pilgrims dress the same?
5.1: The Akhis were brotherhoods of young working men in the towns of Anatolia, linked to the ideal of futuwwa (chivalry). "Nowhere in the world are there to be found any to compare with them in solicitude for strangers" (vol. II, pp. 417-418).
5.2: Ask: how could our family welcome a guest or a newcomer this week?
5.3: Ask: when did someone make you feel welcome in a new place?
5.4: Cook or share a simple meal with a neighbour or a guest together.
5.5: Ask: what can children do to help travellers or new people?
6.1: Look at pictures of old Delhi's buildings together. Ask: what would a traveller from Morocco find new there?
6.2: The Sultan was Muhammad ibn Tughluq. "Do not think that the office of qadi of Dihli is one of the minor functions; it is the highest of functions in our estimation" (vol. III, pp. 746-747). Ibn Battuta replied that he followed the school of Malik while the people there were Hanafis, and did not know the language; the Sultan gave him two deputies.
6.3: The book also tells of this Sultan's great cruelty, and of Ibn Battuta falling out of favour and fearing for his life. In India he was also once seized by raiders, stripped and nearly killed (vol. IV, pp. 776-777). The game leaves these out.
6.4: Ask: when have you had to decide something fairly, like sharing sweets? How did you do it?
7.1: "These islands are one of the wonders of the world and number about two thousand in all" (vol. IV, p. 821). The translator notes that some are mere sandbanks, and rather more than 200 are inhabited.
7.2: "The inhabitants of the Maldives are all of them Muslims, pious and upright" (vol. IV, p. 821). He stayed for a long time and served as a judge there.
7.3: He married several times on his travels, in the Maldives too ("I married several women there", vol. IV, p. 828), and left wives and children behind in more than one country. The game leaves his marriages out.
7.4: If you can, open a coconut together and taste the milk.
7.5: Ask: what do you think it is like to live on a tiny island?
7.6: Ask: what grows near our home? What do we make from it?
8.1: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country. Ask: how do you think Islam came there? (With traders and travellers, like Ibn Battuta.)
8.2: "The people came out to us in little boats bringing coconuts, bananas, mangoes and fish" (vol. IV, p. 875). The city was Sumutra (Samudra-Pasai, in today's Aceh), which later gave its name to the whole island.
8.3: Ask: what gift would you bring to welcome someone?
8.4: Sultan al-Malik al-Zahir: "one of the noblest and most generous of kings, a Shafi'i ... a lover of jurists, who come to his audiences for the recitation of the Qur'an and for discussions" (vol. IV, p. 876). The book also says he often fought the unbelievers around him; the game leaves that out.
8.5: "He is unassuming and walks to the Friday prayer on foot" (vol. IV, p. 876). Greeting there was by shaking hands.
8.6: Ask: what does it mean to be humble? Who do you know who is humble?
9.1: Ask: how far is China from Morocco? Trace the journey on a map.
9.2: Paper money: "pieces of paper the size of the palm of the hand" (vol. IV, p. 889).
9.3: Look at real money together, coins and notes. Which is made of paper?
9.4: Look at a china dish or cup at home together. Where was it made?
9.5: "China is the safest and best country for the traveller" (vol. IV, p. 892). Historians doubt that he went as far north as he says: the translator quotes Henry Yule, "one's doubts arise whether Ibn Batuta could have travelled beyond Hang-chau" (vol. IV, p. 905, n. 58).
9.6: Ask: what makes a place safe for travellers?
10.1: Ask: how would you feel coming home after a very long time?
10.2: "I reached the city of Taza, where I learnt that my mother had died of the plague, God Most High have mercy upon her" (vol. IV, p. 924). It was the Black Death of 1348-49. On the way, in Damascus, he had learnt that his father had died fifteen years before (vol. IV, p. 915).
10.3: Make a dua together for family members who have passed away: Allahumma ighfir lahum warhamhum.
10.4: He reached Fez at the end of Sha'ban 750, November 1349 (vol. IV, pp. 924-925).
10.5: Ask your child to tell the way home in their own words.
11.1: Ask: what do you need to cross a desert? (Water, camels, a guide, patience.)
11.2: Look at the Sahara on a map. Ask: how big is it compared to our country?
11.3: "Among their good practices are their avoidance of injustice; there is no people more averse to it ... the universal security in their country, for neither the traveller nor the resident there has to fear thieves or bandits" (vol. IV, p. 964). The Sultan was Mansa Sulayman, brother of Mansa Musa.
11.4: "They dress in clean white clothes on Fridays; if one of them has only a threadbare shirt he washes it and cleans it and wears it for prayer on Friday" (vol. IV, p. 965).
11.5:
"They pay great attention to memorizing the Holy Qur'an. If their children appear to be backward in learning it they put shackles on them and do not remove them till they learn it." He saw the qadi's children shackled on the day of Eid, and a well-dressed young man with a heavy shackle on his foot (vol. IV, p. 965). The game says only that the children worked hard.

He also listed "bad practices" in Mali: servant women and slave-girls who went unclothed, people putting dust on their heads before the Sultan, and eating carrion, dogs and donkeys (vol. IV, pp. 965-966). These are a Moroccan judge's views of a culture not his own.
11.6: Ibn Juzayy wrote the book in Fez in 1355-56 from what Ibn Battuta told him, at the order of the Sultan Abu 'Inan. Scholars think some passages were borrowed from earlier writers, and that he may not have reached every place he describes (Ross Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta, 1986, discusses this). He died in Morocco around 1368.
11.7: Ask your child to retell the whole journey. Which place would they most like to visit?
